1  Introduction

Medical knowledge and capabilities of language models have advanced rapidly, yet their deployment remains centralized. Among open-weight medical systems, strong models such as MedGemma-27B-text-it [1] still require substantial accelerator memory for practical deployment, while proprietary medical systems such as Med-PaLM-style models and large GPT-4-based clinical assistants are typically accessed through cloud infrastructure. Both fundamentally conflict with the privacy, latency, and reliability requirements of healthcare. Patient records, symptom descriptions, and clinical notes are protected health information governed by strict regulatory regimes (HIPAA, GDPR, and equivalents). The dominant cloud paradigm requires this data to leave the device, traverse network infrastructure, and be processed remotely, creating attack surfaces, compliance burdens, and a fundamental tension between AI capability and patient privacy.

The compact-medical gap.

The current open landscape has a sharp trade-off between capability and deployability. MedGemma-27B-text-it delivers strong medical performance, but at 27B parameters it is infeasible for edge deployment, requiring tens of GB of VRAM. MedGemma-1.5-4B-it [2] is technically runnable on a high-end laptop but lacks the domain-specific capabilities of its larger variant on medical benchmarks, and, to the best of our knowledge, no open model in the 1–4B range delivers accuracy comparable to large medical-model baselines. This is not a pure compression problem: smaller models trained with conventional recipes suffer disproportionately on knowledge-intensive medical tasks, where factual precision and safe, well-structured responses are essential. Nor does fitting device memory guarantee efficient inference: compact reasoning models can still overthink, producing long traces that increase sequential decoding latency, energy use, and KV-cache traffic.

Our thesis.

For compact medical LLMs, medical capability and deployment efficiency can be optimized jointly: high-quality synthetic supervision and staged post-training build accuracy, while length-aware alignment and quantization reduce generation and memory costs for private on-device use. We test this thesis by constructing the MedPsy11 1 In MedPsy, “Med” denotes the medical specialization, while “Psy” is the shared suffix used across our organization’s model families, inspired by psychohistory in Isaac Asimov’s fiction rather than psychology. family of two text-only medical models, MedPsy-1.7B and MedPsy-4B22 2 Models and supporting artifacts are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/qvac/medpsy., on top of Qwen3 backbones [3] with a four-stage post-training recipe (two Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stages over a synthetic medical corpus built from public Genesis III biology/medicine seed prompts [4] and newly generated health seeds derived from FineFineWeb [5], then two Reinforcement Learning (RL) stages with hard-sample mining inspired by Fleming-R1 [6]), and we evaluate them across eight benchmark suites spanning clinical exams (MedQA-USMLE [7], MedMCQA [8]), health literacy (MMLU-Health, MMLU-Pro Health [9, 10]), expert reasoning (MedXpertQA [11]), biomedical research (PubMedQA [12]), underserved-region medicine (AfriMedQA [13]), and real-world clinical scenarios (HealthBench and HealthBench-Hard [14]).

Contributions.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    State-of-the-Art Efficient Models. MedPsy-4B matches MedGemma-27B on closed-ended accuracy and surpasses on HealthBench suites both MedGemma-4B (+20/+28.33) and 27B (+9.0/+15.3). Similarly, MedPsy-1.7B exceeds MedGemma-4B on closed-ended tasks and outperforms both MedGemma variants on HealthBench, achieving these leads at up to 16×\times smaller scale (Fig. 1(a); Sec. 5).

  • •

    Post-training recipe. We combine single-teacher synthetic supervision, broad-to-focused SFT, and easy-to-hard DAPO with deterministic failure mining. Component ablations separate the roles of SFT, DAPO’s drift-enabling changes, the overlong-response penalty, and Stage-2 mining (Sec. 5.4; App. A.17).

  • •

    Token efficiency for the edge. MedPsy-4B and MedPsy-1.7B achieve 3.2×\times and 1.7×\times token reductions over Qwen3 backbones, significantly lowering on-device latency (Sec. 5.5). This efficiency stems from RL-side compression, primarily a soft overlong-response penalty that maintains accuracy while ensuring the training curriculum remains Pareto-dominant (App. A.17.2).

  • •

    Quantized edge deployment. At Q4_K_M, both model sizes retain aggregate score within one point of BF16 while reducing disk footprint by 68–69%. On-device measurements connect MedPsy-4B’s shorter generations to 75% lower median latency and estimated energy per answer at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB in the tested laptop and smartphone configurations. A broader six-format study identifies a capacity-vs-precision effect at matched footprint (Sec. 5.6; App. A.12).

2  Related Work

Medical LLMs. Med-PaLM [15] and Med-PaLM-2 [16] demonstrated that domain-specialized fine-tuning of large general LLMs could reach passing scores on USMLE-style exams, but they remain proprietary and large. Among open models, the strongest medical performance has largely come from substantially larger systems, such as MedGemma-27B [1], Meditron 70B-scale models [17], and OpenBioLLM-70B [18]; smaller medical models such as MedGemma-1.5-4B-it [2] and JSL-MedLlama-3-8B [19] are more deployable but leave a clear accuracy gap. Based on our evaluation (App. A.3) and to the best of our knowledge, no open model in the 1–4B range matched MedGemma-27B-text-it on closed-ended medical benchmarks or HealthBench prior to our work.

Synthetic data for distillation. Self-instruct and synthetic instruction generation [20, 21] have become standard for scaling supervision. The Genesis III project [4] focused on synthetic data for pre-training, combining seed acquisition, quality filtering, and a “scaling Q&A” stage to produce broad educational corpora. We adapt this pipeline for medical post-training: selected Genesis III question/option fields and a new FineFineWeb-derived health slice are used as prompt seeds, and the resulting scaling-QA material is converted into SFT supervision by generating fresh medical reasoning targets with a stronger teacher model.

RL for medical reasoning. Fleming-R1 [6] applies a multi-stage GRPO curriculum with hard-sample mining to medical reasoning. AlphaMed [22] releases the curated AlphaMed19K medical RL prompt set together with a binary correctness reward and a pass-at-NN difficulty annotation procedure. We adopt a two-stage curriculum in the spirit of Fleming-R1 and reuse AlphaMed’s pass-at-NN annotation, applied here with each model’s own size-matched SFT-2 policy as the annotator; we switch the optimiser to DAPO [23], a GRPO variant that drops the KL anchor, uses asymmetric clip-higher, dynamically filters zero-variance rollout groups, and adds a soft overlong-response penalty.

Reasoning-model test-time efficiency. Reasoning models improve difficult tasks by generating explicit intermediate computation, but long traces increase decode latency, KV-cache memory [24], and energy use [25], all especially costly on edge hardware. MedPsy targets this trade-off in the medical domain, improving accuracy while reducing generated tokens in compact reasoning models.

Edge LLMs and quantization. Edge deployment depends jointly on compressed model footprint and generation cost: quantization governs storage and memory requirements, while response length directly affects latency and energy consumption. GGUF and llama.cpp [26] support practical quantized inference across consumer hardware. Existing medical LLM studies primarily establish BF16 benchmark accuracy. We complement this literature by jointly evaluating quantized medical accuracy and measured on-device efficiency across two model sizes (Sec. 5.6; App. A.12).

3  Data Methodology

In this section we describe at a high level the data used to post-train MedPsy and the teacher-selection process behind it. The training corpus description here reflects the design principles and the recipe used to train the final models that are evaluated in this paper.

3.1  Training data overview

We explored several data mixtures and post-training methodologies before settling on the recipe used for the final MedPsy models. In total, about 10M synthetic rows of medical and healthcare supervision were generated for the final synthetic corpus. The recipe organizes the data into a two-stage curriculum: a broad-coverage corpus (Corpus 1) followed by a smaller, higher-value clinical-QA corpus (Corpus 2). The two corpora play complementary roles in the SFT curriculum (Sec. 4).

Two principles guided the data construction throughout these ablations:

  • •

    Synthetic datasets. Corpus 1 utilizes broad synthetic prompts derived from two primary sources. First, we extracted the question and answer option fields from four public Genesis III subsets [4]: college_medicine, professional_medicine, college_biology, and high_school_biology. Second, following [4], we use Fleming-R1-32B [6] to generate four multiple-choice questions (MCQs) for each document in the FineFineWeb health sub-domain [5]. We selected Fleming-R1-32B as it achieves strong performance on closed-ended medical tasks while offering higher throughput than larger teacher models. Corpus 2 instead utilizes train splits from focused open-source medical QA datasets as higher-value clinical prompts. Together, these broad synthetic and focused public-train prompts are used as seeds to generate the final synthetic training data.

  • •

    A single, controlled SFT target teacher. Every long-form assistant target used for supervision (chain-of-thought traces, extended rationales, decision-oriented answers) is newly generated by Baichuan-M3-235B [27], the teacher selected in Sec. 3.2, rather than taken from open-source assistant traces. This separation keeps prompt generation and target generation distinct: the seed data controls coverage, while Baichuan-M3-235B provides style adaptation and medical-reasoning knowledge distillation for the SFT targets.

The output of this stage is a curated medical and healthcare post-training corpus that combines synthetic expansion, reasoning-focused data, and public medical QA prompts, all paired with teacher-generated reasoning targets; source list, licenses, and prompts are in App. A.1.

3.2  Teacher selection

Because our supervision is the teacher’s output, the teacher’s ceiling directly bounds the student’s. From a literature review and public medical leaderboards, we identified three strong candidates (Baichuan-M3-235B [27], GPT-OSS-120B [28], and Fleming-R1-32B [6]) and evaluated them on our benchmark suite under three independent model graders (Sec. 5.1). The same suite serves teacher selection and final reporting, as it directly measures the supervision quality the student distills.

Baichuan-M3-235B leads with 74.83 average closed-ended accuracy (vs. 72.73/72.55), with its largest advantages on the most expert-level benchmarks (MedXpertQA: +5.61/+10.98; MMLU-Pro Health: +5.05/+2.73), and beats both alternatives by 6–12 HealthBench points across all three graders (Tables 6, 7). Since the teacher’s clinical reasoning and communication quality is exactly the signal the student distills, this open-ended advantage was decisive: we use Baichuan-M3-235B as the teacher for all final MedPsy training data. A controlled student-level ablation (App. A.2) verifies that this choice transfers when the prompt set, base model, and training pipeline are held fixed.

4  Post-Training Methodology

4.1  Backbone selection

We selected backbones via a controlled comparison at each target size against four other open candidates (full tables in App. A.4). At the 3-4B class, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 leads closed-ended by +13.43 over Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, +14.11 over SmolLM3-3B, and +20.51 over gemma-3-4b-it, and dominates HealthBench by +21–26 points over Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across all three graders. At the sub-2B class, Qwen3-1.7B (Thinking) leads by +5.81 over the next-best closed-ended backbone (LFM2.5-1.2B-Thinking), remains ahead of LFM2.5-1.2B-Thinking across all three HealthBench graders, and is +21–26 points ahead of Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on HealthBench. We therefore build MedPsy-4B on top of Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and MedPsy-1.7B on Qwen3-1.7B (with enable_thinking=True); an architecture summary of both backbones is given in App. A.6.

4.2  Four-stage curriculum

The four stages are:

  1. 1.

    SFT Stage 1: broad medical adaptation (Corpus 1). The model absorbs large-scale synthetic supervision spanning biology, medicine, and health, building wide factual coverage and medical vocabulary.

  2. 2.

    SFT Stage 2: reasoning specialization (Corpus 2). The model shifts to a smaller set of high-value clinical QA examples with teacher-generated CoT, sharpening answer structure and clinical reasoning depth.

  3. 3.

    RL Stage 1: consolidation on easy/moderate cases. DAPO [23] on ∼\sim16K examples from AlphaMed19K [22], initialized from the SFT-stage-2 checkpoint. This stage reinforces correct chains of reasoning on clinical scenarios where the model already has partial competence.

  4. 4.

    RL Stage 2: hard-enriched targeting. The full set is re-annotated with the best Stage-1 checkpoint and a hard-enriched subset of ∼\sim2–4K items is built deterministically at a fixed 1:2 right-to-wrong ratio. The purpose of Stage 2 is to push the model on its persistent failure modes.

Our RL phase builds on three lines of prior work. The two-stage RLVR-with-curriculum framework, consolidating reasoning on easier cases before targeting persistent failures, follows Fleming-R1 [6]. The Stage-1 corpus, the pass-at-NN difficulty annotation procedure, and the binary correctness reward are inspired by AlphaMed [22]. The structured <think>/<answer> reasoning trace and the idea of conditioning the reward on the presence of a reasoning block follow Med-U1 [29] (and DeepSeek-R1-Zero [30] more broadly). We adopt the structured <think>/<answer> format and extend the binary correctness signal to a four-tier gated reward (§4.2); a controlled ablation (App. A.17.1) shows the four-tier extension is essentially neutral on accuracy versus a binary reward and provides only a modest token-efficiency benefit at 4B, so we report it as a design choice rather than a primary contribution. Within this scaffolding, our two RL design contributions are: a single-pass deterministic Stage-2 mining procedure (§4.2), and the integration of all four stages into a single training pipeline targeted at the sub-7B medical reasoning regime.

Difficulty annotation and Stage-1 data.

Following AlphaMed, we annotate every training prompt empirically by sampling N=5N{=}5 rollouts at temperature 0.70.7 from the policy and labelling by the count ncn_{c} of correct answers, mapped to six difficulty levels L1L_{1}–L6L_{6} (L1=5/5L_{1}{=}5/5, L6=0/5L_{6}{=}0/5); the coarser Easy/Moderate/Difficult split groups L1L_{1} alone, L2L_{2}–L5L_{5} together, and L6L_{6} alone. The Stage-1 training set follows AlphaMed’s data recipe: all of MedQA plus per-level stratified sampling of MedMCQA (capped at 1,600 per LiL_{i}), with PubMedQA omitted following AlphaMed’s finding that it harms reasoning transfer. From this, ∼\sim16K items at the Easy/Moderate levels form the actual Stage-1 corpus.

Reasoning-aware reward.

The model is required to emit reasoning inside <think>...</think> tags and a final answer letter inside <answer>...</answer> [29, 30]. Let c∈{0,1}c\in\{0,1\} indicate answer correctness (matching ground truth) and t∈{0,1}t\in\{0,1\} indicate the presence of a non-trivial reasoning block. Our task reward generalises the binary correctness/format scheme of Med-U1 to a four-tier function that gates jointly on cc and tt:

rtask​(c,t)={1.0if c=1,t=1(correct + reasoning)0.5if c=1,t=0(correct, no reasoning; “shortcut”)0.1if c=0,t=1(reasoning, wrong answer; partial credit)0.0otherwise(no valid structure).r_{\text{task}}(c,t)\;=\;\begin{cases}1.0&\text{if }c=1,t=1\quad(\text{correct }+\text{ reasoning})\\ 0.5&\text{if }c=1,t=0\quad(\text{correct, no reasoning; ``shortcut''})\\ 0.1&\text{if }c=0,t=1\quad(\text{reasoning, wrong answer; partial credit})\\ 0.0&\text{otherwise}\quad(\text{no valid structure}).\end{cases} (1)

The 0.5 vs. 1.0 split actively penalises the shortcut of skipping reasoning even when the model happens to answer correctly; the 0.1 tier supplies a non-zero gradient on rollout groups where no candidate is correct, partially mitigating reward sparsity on Difficult items.

Single-pass deterministic Stage-2 mining.

Fleming-R1 adapts the Stage-2 distribution through iterative re-evaluation. We instead perform a single deterministic mining pass: after Stage 1, the best Stage-1 checkpoint is re-evaluated on the full 19K-item set with the same pass-at-NN procedure; items that the policy still fails on every attempt (nc=0n_{c}{=}0) are retained in full, and a smaller sample of items it gets right is added to enforce a 1:2 right-to-wrong ratio.33 3 Concretely, our 4B Stage-2 set contains 2,439 items (4.7% of the original set was still “Difficult” after Stage 1), and the 1.7B Stage-2 set contains 4,317 items (8.3% Difficult after Stage 1).

Optimization.

Both RL stages use DAPO [23], a GRPO variant whose actor objective drops the KL-to-reference term and replaces PPO’s symmetric clip ϵ\epsilon with an asymmetric (ϵlow,ϵhigh)(\epsilon_{\text{low}},\epsilon_{\text{high}}):

ℒDAPO​(θ)=−𝔼(s,a)∼πθold​[min⁡(ρt​(θ)​A^t,clip⁡(ρt​(θ), 1−ϵlow, 1+ϵhigh)​A^t)],\mathcal{L}_{\text{DAPO}}(\theta)\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}}\!\left[\,\min\!\Big(\rho_{t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{t},\;\;\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\rho_{t}(\theta),\,1-\epsilon_{\text{low}},\,1+\epsilon_{\text{high}}\right)\hat{A}_{t}\Big)\right], (2)

where ρt​(θ)=πθ​(at|st)/πθold​(at|st)\rho_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}|s_{t}) and A^t\hat{A}_{t} is the GRPO group-relative advantage computed from n=16n=16 rollouts per prompt. We use ϵlow=0.2\epsilon_{\text{low}}=0.2, ϵhigh=0.28\epsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28 (clip-higher) and dynamic filtering of zero-variance rollout groups (those for which all nn rollouts share the same reward, i.e. the advantage is identically zero). On top of rtaskr_{\text{task}} in Eq. 1 we apply a soft overlong-response penalty over a Lsoft=2,048L_{\text{soft}}{=}2{,}048-token buffer within an Lmax=4,096L_{\text{max}}{=}4{,}096-token response budget:

roverlong​(L)=−λ​max⁡(0,L−LsoftLmax−Lsoft),λ=1,r_{\text{overlong}}(L)\;=\;-\,\lambda\,\max\!\left(0,\;\frac{L-L_{\text{soft}}}{L_{\text{max}}-L_{\text{soft}}}\right),\qquad\lambda{=}1, (3)

where LL is the per-rollout response length in tokens. The total per-rollout reward is r=rtask+roverlongr=r_{\text{task}}+r_{\text{overlong}}. Sequences that reach LmaxL_{\text{max}} receive the full −λ-\lambda, while sequences below LsoftL_{\text{soft}} are unpenalised. Per-stage hyperparameters are in App. A.7; Algorithm 1 summarises the full pipeline.

This broad-then-focused design mirrors the SFT curriculum and is especially important in medicine, where strong average accuracy can mask weaknesses on rare or complex cases. Full training configurations/hyperparameters for SFT/RL and compute requirements are reported in Appendix A.7. The recipe is not Qwen3-specific: applying all four stages to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [30], a Qwen2.5-derived reasoning checkpoint, lifts the seven-task closed-ended average from 28.4 to 52.2 and HealthBench from 7.0 to 58.0 (App. A.5).

5  Evaluation

5.1  Methodology

Generation protocol. Unless otherwise noted, each model is evaluated with the generation parameters recommended for that model, and every reported evaluation is run three times with the arithmetic mean reported. For MedPsy and the Qwen3 baselines we use temperature=0.6, top_k=20, top_p=0.95, and max_output_tokens=16384.

Closed-ended (LLM-as-Parser). For all closed-ended benchmarks (MMLU-Health, MMLU-Pro Health, MedMCQA, MedQA-USMLE, MedXpertQA, AfriMedQA, PubMedQA), we use an LLM-as-Parser evaluation implemented in OpenCompass [31]. MMLU-Health is reported as the averaged accuracy across six MMLU sub-domains: anatomy, clinical_knowledge, college_biology, college_medicine, medical_genetics, and professional_medicine. The student model generates its full unconstrained response (with reasoning), and a separate reasoning model parses the final selected option, which is exact-matched against ground truth. This decouples generation from evaluation, avoiding both the suppression of reasoning that comes with letter-only constrained decoding and the false negatives that plague regex-based extraction. Main closed-ended tables use QwQ [32] as the parser; an example parser prompt is in App. A.1. To estimate parser sensitivity, we re-scored the same generations with three independent parsers (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [33], GPT-OSS-120B [28], and QwQ); the maximum parser-induced average-score spread is only 0.45 points across all evaluated models, with stable model rankings and coherent per-benchmark differences (App. A.11).

HealthBench (physician-authored rubrics with model-based grading). HealthBench [14] evaluates 5,000 realistic health conversations using 48,562 conversation-specific criteria written by 262 physicians. Each criterion specifies what a response should include or avoid and carries a physician-assigned importance weight; model graders apply this fixed expert-authored standard to each response. The benchmark’s model-grading protocol was validated against physician judgments. We evaluate with three independent grader families (CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct [34], Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [33], and GPT-OSS-120B [28]) to test whether conclusions depend on a particular grader. Table 2 reports all three directly, while per-dimension breakdowns use CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct (App. A.9). Three-grader results for teacher and backbone selection are reported in App. A.2–A.4. HealthBench-Hard is the hardest subset, requiring multi-step reasoning, complex safety judgments, and expert-level clinical knowledge.

Train–test decontamination. To account for overlaps in public medical datasets, we reran the closed-ended evaluation after excluding matched benchmark test items. Decontamination removed 157157 examples (1.10%1.10\%) without altering model rankings (App. A.11).

5.2  Closed-ended results

MedPsy-4B matches MedGemma-27B-text-it in aggregate closed-ended performance (70.54 vs. 69.95; +0.59) at 6.75×\times smaller scale. A matched-instance analysis following Medmarks v0.1.0 [35] likewise finds near parity across three runs (50.25% versus 49.75%; App. A.11). Compared to its own backbone, post-training adds +7.44 average. The lead is not explained by parser choice or train–test overlap: the ranking is stable across three closed-ended parsers and remains after decontamination (App. A.11). MedPsy-1.7B reaches 62.62, beating MedGemma-1.5-4B-it by +11.42 and matching Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 at less than half its size; the largest gains over MedGemma-1.5-4B are MMLU-Health (+15.03) and MedQA-USMLE (+10.66). PubMedQA is a known ceiling case: the Qwen3-1.7B backbone already scores 72.33, so the 1.7B post-training trades −2.80-2.80 on PubMedQA for double-digit gains elsewhere; the 4B model avoids this regression and improves PubMedQA to 75.00. Accuracy also carries over to much longer inputs: on LongHealth [36] (5,090–6,754-word clinical documents), MedPsy-4B scores 0.855/0.875 on Tasks 1/2, above MedGemma-27B-text-it (0.828/0.802), and MedPsy-1.7B leads MedGemma-1.5-4B-it by up to 30.6 points (App. A.16).

5.3  HealthBench results

HealthBench complements closed-ended accuracy by evaluating responses to realistic, open-ended clinical scenarios against fixed, conversation-specific physician-authored rubrics. Its seven dimensions cover expertise-tailored communication, response depth, context seeking, emergency referrals, global health, health-data tasks, and responding under uncertainty. Table 2 reports Standard and Hard scores under all three grader families.

MedPsy-4B ranks first on every (grader, split) cell of Tab. 2, and MedPsy-1.7B is second-best across the board, surpassing MedGemma-27B-text-it on both Standard and Hard under all three graders. Absolute scores vary with grader strictness, but the complete five-model ordering is identical across all six grader-by-split cells, and the Hard-split lead is uniformly larger than the Standard-split lead under every grader. The gains therefore do not depend on the calibration of a single model grader (cross-grader consistency summary in App. A.8).

A per-dimension breakdown under CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct is reported in App. A.9: MedPsy-4B leads on all seven dimensions in both Standard and Hard evaluations, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses MedGemma-27B-text-it on all seven HealthBench-Hard dimensions.

5.4  Stage-wise progression

Several patterns are consistent across both sizes (Table 3). SFT Stage 1 delivers the largest single jump (+7.53 / +4.83), confirming that broad medical exposure from Corpus 1 is the foundation; gains are most dramatic on HealthBench (+17.33 / +11.00) and MedQA-USMLE (+16.79 / +11.47). SFT Stage 2 adds focused reasoning on MedQA-USMLE (+4.79 for 1.7B), MMLU-Pro Health (+3.22 for 1.7B), and MedXpertQA (+2.49 for 4B). The two RL stages together provide the final sharpening, peaking on MedQA-USMLE (+6.29 for 1.7B) and MedMCQA (+5.02 / +2.94), the benchmarks that most reward structured clinical reasoning. Stage 2 hard-mining accounts for essentially all of the released model’s MedXpertQA lift: replacing the mined Stage-2 set with a uniformly-random subset of identical size loses 5.05.0 pp (4B) and 2.02.0 pp (1.7B) on MedXpertQA, while easy/medium benchmarks are essentially unchanged (App. A.17.1). HealthBench gains are installed early: SFT Stage 1 already lifts HealthBench to its final level, and the RL stages preserve it while improving closed-ended accuracy and token efficiency.

5.5  Token efficiency

Sample-weighted across all eight benchmarks, the 4B model achieves a 3.2×\times reduction in average response length (909 vs. 2,953 tokens for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507) while improving accuracy, and the 1.7B model a 1.7×\times reduction (1,110 vs. 1,901 tokens for Qwen3-1.7B Thinking). Complementing these observed length reductions, an explicit thinking-budget sweep shows that MedPsy-4B retains 96.6% of its unbounded closed-ended score with a 300-token thinking cap (App. A.14). The 1.7B reduction is smaller because its backbone already emits shorter outputs, and on HealthBench MedPsy-1.7B writes slightly longer responses than its backbone, trading tokens for the +17 HealthBench points of Sec. 5.4. The per-benchmark breakdown is in App. A.10 (Tab. 20).

We decompose the RL-side compression into three independently controllable mechanisms in App. A.17.2: vanilla GRPO with a KL anchor compresses by only ∼6\sim 6–2020%, switching to DAPO’s drift-enabling modifications (KL-removal and asymmetric clip-higher) brings compression to ∼44\sim 44–4545%, and adding the soft overlong-response penalty pushes it to the released-model ∼65\sim 65–6666%. The ordering of the RL stages compounds this: Stage 1 trains on items typically answerable with short reasoning, installing a low-token-budget habit; Stage 2 then pushes accuracy on hard items starting from this already-compressed checkpoint and preserves the short-reasoning habit.

5.6  Quantization for mobile deployment

To meet mobile RAM constraints, we convert both models to GGUF with llama.cpp [26] and evaluate six quantization formats spanning 8-, 4-, and 3-bit precision. This sweep identifies Q4_K_M as the preferred deployment configuration, offering the strongest observed balance between footprint reduction and full-suite score retention at both model sizes. Table 4 reports the complete per-format comparison together with the real-device profile at Q4_K_M; the imatrix ablation and per-benchmark details are in App. A.12.

Q4_K_M accuracy and footprint. At Q4_K_M, both model sizes reduce disk footprint by 68–69% while keeping aggregate score within one point of BF16 (Table 4(a)). MedPsy-4B reaches 2.6 GB with a 0.81-point aggregate-score change, while MedPsy-1.7B reaches 1.2 GB with a 0.73-point change. Across the broader six-format study, the 4B model retains strong accuracy through 3-bit quantization, and the matched-footprint comparison reveals a capacity-vs-precision effect: the 2.0 GB IQ3_M 4B model outperforms the 2.1 GB Q8_0 1.7B model (Table 4(a)). At matched on-disk size, allocating storage to more parameters at lower precision buys more performance than fewer parameters at higher precision.

Full quantization landscape. Beyond Q4_K_M, the six-format comparison (Table 4(a); Fig. 1(b)) shows that Q8_0 is near-lossless at both sizes (−-0.15 and 0.00 aggregate-score change at roughly half the footprint). The I-quants trade precision for footprint gracefully at 4B: IQ4_NL and IQ4_XS lose 1.0–1.1 points, and IQ3_M (2.0 GB) loses only 1.50 while exactly matching the BF16 HealthBench-Hard score of 58. Collapse occurs only at IQ3_XXS (−-5.56 at 4B, −-12.46 at 1.7B), and even this worst configuration (64.42 closed-ended, 69 HealthBench) remains above the unquantized Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 backbone (63.10/63) and MedGemma-1.5-4B-it (51.20/54). The 1.7B model degrades roughly twice as fast as the 4B below 4-bit precision, consistent with the intuition that smaller models have less weight redundancy: every channel carries more of the model’s behavior, so precision lost per channel translates more directly into degraded reasoning. We therefore do not recommend any sub-4-bit variant of MedPsy-1.7B for medical use.

Real-device deployment. At matched Q4_K_M quantization, MedPsy-4B and its Qwen3 backbone have comparable per-token decode rates, while MedPsy-4B generates 73% fewer tokens per answer. This translates to 74.7% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer on the Apple M5 Pro, with 4.29 GB peak RAM (Table 4(b)). A separate 8K-context stress test records 4.83 GB as the largest laptop peak for MedPsy-4B Q4_K_M (App. A.15). Measurements on a OnePlus 13 confirm fully local execution at 2.22 GB peak RAM for MedPsy-1.7B and 3.98 GB for MedPsy-4B; full protocols and measurements are in App. A.13.

6  Discussion and Limitations

The results support our central thesis: for compact medical LLMs, medical capability and deployment efficiency can be optimized jointly. In MedPsy, broad SFT establishes medical coverage, focused SFT improves clinical reasoning, and hard-sample RL sharpens the most reasoning-heavy benchmarks (Sec. 5.4). The full curriculum (SFT→\toSFT→\toRL Stage 1→\toRL Stage 2) is also strictly Pareto-dominant over single-stage hard-only RL on token-vs-accuracy (best performance at ∼3\sim 3–4×4\times shorter response length) (App. A.17.2). The Easy/Moderate Stage 1 leaves the policy already compressed and high-reward before Stage 2 mining targets residual hard items, preserving response compression even in the more challenging scenarios that require longer reasoning.

However, these findings should be interpreted within several important boundaries: the models are text-only; the training data is predominantly English. Like all LLMs, the models can produce confident but incorrect medical statements; they should not be used for autonomous diagnosis or treatment. Real clinical decision support would require additional safety review, IRB-grade evaluation, prospective testing, and regulatory clearance.

7  Conclusion and Future Work

These limitations point to several directions for future work. The recipe should be extended to multilingual and multimodal medical settings, and evaluation should move beyond the current benchmark suite. In particular, compact medical models need stronger open-ended evaluations, safety benchmarks, and medical error detection tests before their behavior can be understood in higher-risk clinical scenarios.

Within this scope, MedPsy shows that compact, text-only medical LLMs (1.7B and 4B) can match or surpass much larger medical models: MedPsy-4B matches MedGemma-27B on closed-ended benchmarks at 6.75×\times smaller scale, and both sizes surpass it on HealthBench-Hard. Both run fully locally within 5 GB of peak RAM on the tested laptop and smartphone, where shorter generations cut median latency and estimated energy per answer by 75%. A controlled synthetic-data pipeline, a broad-then-focused SFT curriculum, and hard-sample RL deliver strong medical accuracy and improved token efficiency (1.71.7–3.2×3.2\times fewer generated tokens) at small scale. The quantization study further shows that Q4_K_M keeps aggregate score within one point of BF16 at a 68–69% smaller footprint, while very low precision exposes a clear capacity-vs-precision trade-off. Overall, MedPsy suggests that for compact medical LLMs, data quality, staged post-training, and alignment design dominate parameter scale, and medical capability and deployment efficiency can be optimized jointly.

Appendix A Technical appendices and supplementary material

Appendix contents

A.1  Data sources and prompts

Corpus 1 uses selected Genesis III biology/medicine seeds plus new health seeds. For the health slice, we select FineFineWeb health-domain passages after Ultra-FineWeb-classifier[37] filtering and apply the scaling-QA prompt below to generate self-contained MCQ user prompts. We keep only the question/options as the user turn, then use Baichuan-M3-235B to generate every assistant target; Corpus 2 uses only the public train sources listed in Tab. 5 as the user turn, then uses Baichuan-M3-235B as well to generate every assistant target.

Scaling-QA prompt for new health-domain seeds.

The prompt template used for generating samples starting from the seeds is as follows:

⬇
You are a {{level}} {{domain}} tutor. I will give you a context passage.
IGNORE the details of the passage. Use it only as inspiration for topics, but DO NOT refer to the passage, book, text, or "discussed/mentioned" material in your questions.
Context:
{{output}}
Generate EXACTLY 4 independent, self-contained questions suitable for {{level}} level {{domain}}.
Output rules (MUST be followed strictly):
- Output EXACTLY 4 samples.
- Each row = ONE question in the following format:
"<question>","<choiceA>","<choiceB>","<choiceC>","<choiceD>","<correct_choice_letter>"
- Each row MUST end with a newline (line break).
- Do NOT join multiple questions into one line.
- Do NOT output any extra text, headers, or blank lines.
Field definitions:
- <question> = a fully self-contained {{level}}-level {{domain}} problem.
It must NOT reference any passage, book, figure, table, or "as discussed" or "as mentioned" style wording.
Include all necessary values, constants, or definitions directly inside the question.
- <choiceA> ... <choiceD> = four mutually exclusive, plausible answer choices.
- <correct_choice_letter> = exactly one of A, B, C, D.
Question variety:
- Use a mix of imperative (e.g., "Calculate..."), interrogative, completion/fill-in, and true/false style.
- Do NOT start all questions with the same word.
- Include realistic values/constants when needed (e.g., g = 9.8 m/s^2).
- Use standard SI units and symbols.
Hard constraints:
- Generate exactly 4 questions (4 samples).
- Correct answers must be evenly distributed: one A, one B, one C, one D.
- Randomize placement of correct answers; no clustering.
- Each row must contain exactly 6 comma-separated values.
- Do NOT add quotes around the entire block; only around individual fields.
Output ONLY the 4 samples in the required format, nothing else.
Closed-ended answer-extraction prompt.

This is the MMLU extractor; the same template was used for each closed-ended dataset, changing only the option list and dataset-specific field names.

⬇
MMLU_ANSWER_EXTRACTOR_TEMPLATE = """
You are an expert answer extractor. Your ONLY job is to extract the final answer from the candidate’s response.
CRITICAL INSTRUCTIONS - READ CAREFULLY:
- DO NOT solve the question yourself
- DO NOT generate a new answer
- DO NOT think about what the correct answer should be
- DO NOT evaluate whether the candidate’s answer is right or wrong
- ONLY extract what the candidate actually wrote as their final answer
Your task is purely extraction, not generation or evaluation.
Here are the extraction guidelines for MMLU multiple choice questions:
1. Look for the candidate’s final answer in their response. This should be one of: A, B, C, or D
- Look for explicit statements like "ANSWER: A", "The answer is B", "Final answer: C"
- Look for \boxed{A} format (extract what’s inside the braces)
- Look for standalone letters A, B, C, or D in their conclusion
- The final choice they settle on in their reasoning
2. If the candidate’s response contains multiple different answers:
- If they state one answer but then correct/fix themselves, extract the corrected/final answer they provided
- If they state multiple different answers without choosing one or correcting themselves, return "MULTIPLE_ANSWERS"
3. If you cannot clearly identify a single letter choice (A, B, C, or D) in the response, return "NO_ANSWER"
4. If the candidate generates new questions:
- DO NOT extract the answer from the new generated questions
- ONLY extract the answer from the original question
RESPONSE FORMAT:
First, provide a brief explanation of why you are extracting that particular answer (what indicators you found in the candidate’s response).
Then, provide the extracted answer as a single letter.
Use this exact format:
Extraction Reasoning: [Brief explanation of what indicators led you to extract this answer from the candidate’s response]
Extracted Candidate’s Answer: [A single letter: A, B, C, or D. Use MULTIPLE_ANSWERS if the candidate provided multiple different answers, or NO_ANSWER if no clear answer was found.]
<Original Question Begin>:
Question: {input}
A. {A}
B. {B}
C. {C}
D. {D}
Answer:
<Original Question End>
<Candidate’s Response Begin>:
{prediction}
<Candidate’s Response End>
"""

A.2  Teacher-selection ablation

This appendix details the ablation study performed to determine the most effective teacher model for our distillation pipeline. We evaluate candidate models across several closed-ended medical benchmarks in Table 6 and report their overall HealthBench performance across three distinct graders in Table 7.

As shown in the results, Baichuan-M3-235B consistently outperforms the other candidates, which justifies its selection as the primary teacher for our experiments.

Student-level validation of teacher choice.

To test whether the teacher-level HealthBench advantage transfers to the student, we trained three controlled 4B SFT arms from the same base model on the same 170K-prompt subset with the same training pipeline, changing only the source of the target responses. Table 8 reports the results.

Closed-ended averages differ by at most 0.41 points, whereas HealthBench separates the arms by 11 points. Mixing heterogeneous target teachers provides no benefit here: the mixed arm (60.0) tracks the Fleming-only arm (59.5) rather than the midpoint of the two single-teacher arms (65.25), consistent with a less coherent SFT signal. In this controlled run, the Baichuan-only arm therefore best preserves the open-ended criterion used for teacher selection.

A.3  Additional large medical baselines

Table 9 reports the closed-ended benchmark comparison against additional open medical LLMs in the 8–70B range.

A.4  Backbone-selection ablation

We evaluated multiple candidate backbones at each target size on our full medical benchmark suite before any post-training. Tables 10, 11, 12, 13 report the results.

Among the tested sub-2B candidates, Qwen3-1.7B provided the strongest pretrained starting point across the closed-ended suite and all three HealthBench graders, motivating its selection for the final model.

A.5  Transfer to a Qwen2.5-derived reasoning checkpoint

To test the portability of our post-training recipe beyond Qwen3, we applied the same four-stage pipeline to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [30], a compact reasoning model built on Qwen2.5-Math and distilled from DeepSeek-R1. Table 14 shows consistent gains at every training stage on both the seven closed-ended benchmarks and HealthBench, demonstrating that the recipe also transfers effectively to a Qwen2.5-derived reasoning checkpoint.

Evaluation behavior.

During evaluation, we observed that DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B behaves differently depending on whether the prompt explicitly requests step-by-step reasoning. We therefore report two closed-ended settings: the paper-mirror setting uses the same prompts and answer format as the main experiments, whereas the explicit-reasoning setting adds “Think step by step” and requires the specified final-answer format. The explicit-reasoning setting is applied only to the closed-ended benchmarks; HealthBench is always evaluated under the standard protocol, without any added reasoning instruction or required answer format.

The recipe improves accuracy consistently in both settings. Under the paper-mirror evaluation, the seven-task average rises from 28.42 to 52.16, with gains on all seven tasks; after RL, output length is 33.1% below SFT-2 (1,601 vs. 2,394 tokens). Under explicit reasoning, the average rises from 29.53 to 53.60 while output length falls from 3,007 to 1,476 tokens, a 50.9% reduction. The two settings thus reach comparable final accuracy while exhibiting different length behavior. Under the standard HealthBench protocol, the score rises from 7.0 to 58.0, with output length increasing from 1,292 to 2,089 tokens. Overall, the transfer experiment shows strong gains across both elicitation styles, while explicit prompting primarily changes the token-efficiency profile.

A.6  Backbone architectures

Table 15 summarizes the architectural parameters of the two selected Qwen3 backbones.

A.7  Compute resources

Cluster. 30 worker nodes; 8×\timesNVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 per node; InfiniBand interconnect (Mellanox ConnectX, 8 HCA ports/node); SLURM scheduler. Containers: NVIDIA NeMo 25.09 (Enroot), PyTorch 2.5.1, CUDA 12.1.

Per-job parallelism. 1.7B SFT: 4 nodes, 32 GPUs, TP==1, PP==1, DP==32. 4B SFT: 4 nodes, 32 GPUs, TP==1, PP==1, DP==32.

Training hyperparameters. Both SFT runs used 3 epochs, sequence length 4,096 with packed sequence size 4,096, global batch size 512 packed sequences, and micro batch size 1. Optimization used distributed fused Adam in bf16 mixed precision with a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, minimum learning rate of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, cosine decay, and a linear warmup over 1% of training steps. For RL training, effective per-update batch is 512512 prompts ×\times n=16n{=}16 rollouts =8,192=8{,}192 sampled trajectories. We present the RL configuration in Table 16.

Tracking and checkpoints. Weights & Biases plus TensorBoard. Checkpoints in Megatron torch_dist format (fully parallel save), converted to HuggingFace safetensors for evaluation and deployment.

Training time. The primary experimental pipeline required approximately 8,250 H100 GPU hours. The vast majority of this budget was allocated to the data generation phase (∼\sim8,000 hours), while downstream training stages were significantly less compute-intensive; Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) consumed approximately 100 and 150 hours, respectively. These figures represent the final end-to-end training of our primary model. Including preliminary ablations, failed runs, and evaluation, the total computational expenditure for the project is estimated at approximately 30,000 H100 GPU hours.

A.8  Per-grader HealthBench results

HealthBench’s evaluation criteria are written by physicians; the model graders in our panel determine whether each response satisfies those fixed, conversation-specific criteria. The main paper reports overall scores under all three graders (CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B) directly in Tab. 2. Three-grader results are also reported for the teacher- and backbone-selection ablations (App. A.2, A.4).
Across all four uses of the panel (final-model comparison, teacher ablation, 4B-class backbone ablation, sub-2B-class backbone ablation), the main conclusions are preserved across the three graders: the selected teacher and backbone remain at or near the top, with only a small GPT-OSS swap between the two Qwen3-4B variants, and the released MedPsy models keep the same ordering. Absolute-score levels are uniformly highest under CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct, intermediate under Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and lowest under GPT-OSS-120B (the strictest of the three graders on open-ended clinical content).

A.9  HealthBench per-dimension and per-axis breakdowns

Tab. 17 and Tab. 18 report the per-dimension breakdown of HealthBench (Standard and Hard splits) under CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct, the strongest dedicated model grader on evaluator benchmarks. The seven dimensions are expertise-tailored communication, response depth, context seeking, emergency referrals, global health, health-data tasks, and responding under uncertainty. The Overall column matches the corresponding CompassJudger column of Tab. 2. The 4B model’s strongest dimensions are Emergency Referrals (81.67/62.33), Expertise-Tailored Communication (79.33/55.33), and Responding under Uncertainty (76.33/61.00; Standard/Hard).

Per-axis breakdown.

Where the per-dimension tables show where failures occur, Table 19 shows how response quality deteriorates: it reports the five behavior axes defined by the native HealthBench evaluator. Values are percentages on the 1,000-example Hard split, scored with CompassJudger-2-32B-Instruct and averaged over three independent generation runs. Context Awareness and Instruction Following are the two lowest-scoring axes for both MedPsy model sizes.

A.10  Per-benchmark response length

Table 20 reports the per-benchmark average output length. The first row reports the weighted average; the remaining rows are the per-benchmark values, sorted by Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 response length (descending). Reductions are MedPsy-4B / MedPsy-1.7B versus the corresponding Qwen3 backbone; values <1×<1{\times} indicate that MedPsy produces longer responses than the backbone on that benchmark. The only such case is HealthBench at the 1.7B class (0.9×0.9{\times}), reflecting a deliberate trade for the +17 pp HealthBench gain reported in Sec. 5.4.

A.11  Evaluation Robustness and Decontamination

This appendix provides two robustness checks for the primary closed-ended results. First, we assess parser reliability by re-parsing the original model generations using three independent LLM parsers (Tab. 21). Second, we address potential train–test leakage by rerunning the evaluation suite after excluding test examples that overlap with our final synthetic training corpus (Tabs. 23 and 24).

Decontamination Methodology and Impact.

Although our pipeline utilizes only public training splits, medical datasets are frequently not mutually disjoint. Our audit revealed cross-dataset overlaps: for example, MedQA training items appeared in the MedXpertQA test set, and MedMCQA training items overlapped with AfriMedQA test items. To ensure the integrity of our results, we performed a string-matching decontamination and excluded all overlapping test examples from the final scoring.

The decontaminated results utilize the same checkpoints as the original evaluation; only the overlapping benchmark examples are removed. As shown in the following tables, the percentage of excluded examples is minimal. The impact on performance across all models was found to be negligible, and the relative rankings between our models and the baselines remain unchanged. Full per-benchmark exclusion counts and the resulting decontaminated scores are detailed in Tables 23 and 24.

Matched-instance pairwise comparison.

Following the original Medmarks v0.1.0 implementation [35], we assign one point to the model with the higher reward on each matched example and half a point to each model for a tie, average these scores within each dataset, and combine them using log-dataset-size weighting. The analysis covers AfriMedQA, MMLU-Health, MMLU-Pro Health, MedMCQA, MedQA-USMLE, MedXpertQA, and PubMedQA, with the six MMLU-Health subsets pooled before weighting. The three-run result in Table 22 confirms matching closed-ended performance.

A.12  Quantization: imatrix ablation and per-benchmark tables

This appendix supplements the six-format quantization study of Sec. 5.6, whose per-variant overview is main-paper Table 4, with the Q4_K_M imatrix ablation, the capacity-vs-precision comparison, and per-benchmark closed-ended scores. The comparison uses Q8_0 without imatrix and all sub-8-bit variants (Q4_K_M, IQ4_NL, IQ4_XS, IQ3_M, IQ3_XXS) with imatrix calibration.

On the 1.7B model, imatrix calibration provides its largest closed-ended benefits on the most reasoning-intensive tasks: 4.69 points on MedQA-USMLE, 3.59 on MMLU-Pro Health, and 2.07 on MMLU (Health), the same benchmarks that benefited most from post-training (Sec. 5.4).

The per-variant overall scores for the I-quant variants (IQ4_NL, IQ4_XS, IQ3_M, IQ3_XXS) are reported in main-paper Table 4; Table 25 compares score changes by model size. The imatrix ablation details are split by model size and evaluation type: closed-ended results for 4B and 1.7B are in Tables 26 and 28, and HealthBench per-dimension results are in Tables 27 and 29.

A.13  Real-device measurement protocol

We benchmarked local llama.cpp inference on an Apple M5 Pro using Metal and on a OnePlus 13 (CPH2649IN, Android 16, Adreno 830) using Android build 9226 with Vulkan partial offload (-ngl 20) and six CPU threads. The Apple prompt set contains 20 MedQA and 10 MedXpertQA-Text questions. The phone measurements use three MedQA prompts per model.

Real-device measurements.

We ran the quantized models locally with llama.cpp on an Apple M5 Pro and a OnePlus 13. Table 30 reports the Apple M5 Pro measurements over the 30-prompt set: matched Q4_K_M runs decode at comparable speed (83.9 vs. 82.2 tokens/s), but MedPsy-4B emits 738 rather than 2,727 tokens per answer, reducing median end-to-end time from 34.6 to 8.75 seconds (74.7%). Table 31 reports the OnePlus 13 measurements, where both model sizes run fully locally within 4 GB of measured peak RAM. Estimated energy per answer shows the same pattern: at matched Q4_K_M, MedPsy-4B uses 232 J against the backbone’s 917 J (74.7% lower). The accuracy of these quantized variants on the full benchmark suite is reported in main-paper Table 4.

A.14  Accuracy under explicit thinking budgets

We reran the seven closed-ended tasks with external llama.cpp servers while capping tokens in the explicit thinking channel at 300, 600, 900, or 1,500; when the cap was reached, the runtime injected the instruction “Thinking budget exceeded. Please stop thinking and answer now.” Each condition contains three sampled generations for all 12,549 examples, evaluated with the QwQ parser. Generation uses thinking mode with temperature 0.6, top-kk 20, top-pp 0.95, an 8,192-token output limit, and a 16,384-token sequence limit. Table 32 and Figure 2 reports the resulting average accuracy, the fraction of traces that reached the cap, and the mean length of the final answer channel.

MedPsy-4B retains 96.6%, 98.6%, and 99.3% of its unbounded score at 300, 600, and 900 thinking tokens; Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 reaches 98.2% at 1,500. At 300 tokens, MedPsy-4B scores 8.62 points above the backbone and 4.92 points above the backbone’s unbounded score. These results show stronger accuracy under the tested explicit-reasoning budgets. Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 may move some computation into the answer channel under tighter caps, as suggested by its longer final answers.

A.15  Context-length scaling

On the laptop (Apple M5 Pro, Metal backend), decode throughput at 8K input retains 66.5–72.5% of its 512-token rate across the three tested variants, while peak RAM at 8K remains between 3.16 and 4.83 GB (Table 33); TTFT at 512 tokens is 0.06–0.12 s. These values come from a dedicated context-scaling probe and differ slightly from the smoke-set figures of Table 30; the 4.83 GB peak of MedPsy-4B Q4_K_M at 8K context is the largest peak RAM we observed on the laptop.

These measurements focus on edge context scaling. Table 34 reports a OnePlus 13 CPU run with MedPsy-1.7B Q4_K_M. At 551 and 4,134 input tokens, TTFT is 12.88 and 93.85 seconds, respectively, while decode throughput is 21.07 and 13.88 tokens/s. These measurements provide practical bounds for selecting context budgets on a phone while process RAM remains stable. This sweep uses the CPU build with six threads; Table 31 instead reports generation with partial Vulkan offload (-ngl 20).

A.16  Long-context accuracy on LongHealth

LongHealth [36] evaluates question answering over long clinical documents (5,090–6,754 words), probing the input-length regime in which retrieval-augmented deployment operates. Table 35 reports accuracy on Tasks 1 and 2. Both MedPsy sizes outperform the MedGemma model of the next size class up: MedPsy-4B exceeds MedGemma-27B-text-it by 2.7 and 7.3 points on the two tasks, and MedPsy-1.7B exceeds MedGemma-1.5-4B-it by 2.5 and 30.6 points, indicating that the accuracy reported in the main evaluation carries over to long-context inputs.

A.17  RL ablation studies

We ran a controlled set of ablations to isolate which design choices in the MedPsy RL recipe drive the gains reported in Tables 1–2. Each ablation modifies a single component of the released MedPsy pipeline and trains for the same number of optimisation steps; all other hyperparameters are held constant. The ablations come in two natural groups: (i) effectiveness ablations that probe which components contribute to accuracy, and (ii) token-efficiency ablations that decompose the source of the response-length compression.

Evaluation suite used in this appendix.

For every ablation we score checkpoints on the same three closed-ended benchmarks tracked online during training (MedQA-USMLE, MedXpertQA, PubMedQA) using the lightweight flexible scorer in the inspect-ai evaluation framework [38]. This is a strict subset of the full seven-benchmark suite scored under the LLM-as-Parser methodology of Sec. 5.1 and Table 20; the smoke suite was used to keep ablation compute and time within budget. Per-checkpoint absolute scores in this appendix therefore differ slightly from the LLM-as-Parser numbers in the main paper. For example, on MedQA-USMLE the released MedPsy-4B S2 checkpoint scores 84.84%84.84\% under inspect-ai vs. 84.39%84.39\% under LLM-as-Parser, well within scorer noise. Output-token counts are also broadly consistent across the two scorers but can differ in absolute value due to different prompting conventions and post-generation truncation in the two frameworks; the per-ablation deltas reproduce on both. We use the smoke suite throughout this appendix and direct readers wanting released-checkpoint absolute numbers to the main-paper tables.

Ablation set.

All ablations train from the same SFT-Stage-2 checkpoints used by the released MedPsy models, except RL-from-base, which uses no SFT at all. We use short, descriptive names throughout this appendix:

  • •

    Random S2. Same Stage-2 setup as MedPsy but the training data is a uniformly-random sample from AlphaMed19K [22], sized to match the mined 1:2 right:wrong subset (2,439 items at 4B, 4,317 at 1.7B). Tests whether the mining procedure itself contributes vs. training longer on more data.

  • •

    Binary reward. Replace the four-tier reasoning-aware reward (Eq. 1) with the binary {0,1}\{0,1\} correctness reward used by AlphaMed [22]. Isolates the contribution of the gated reward.

  • •

    No group filter. Disable DAPO’s dynamic filtering of zero-variance rollout groups (filter_groups.enable=false). Isolates the contribution of group filtering.

  • •

    No overlong. Remove the soft penalty applied to responses exceeding Lsoft=2,048L_{\text{soft}}{=}2{,}048 tokens within the Lmax=4,096L_{\text{max}}{=}4{,}096-token budget; all other DAPO settings unchanged. Isolates the contribution of the soft length penalty.

  • •

    Vanilla GRPO. Replace DAPO with vanilla GRPO [39]: re-introduce the KL anchor (kl_coef=0.001=0.001), use symmetric PPO clipping (ϵlow=ϵhigh=0.2\epsilon_{\text{low}}{=}\epsilon_{\text{high}}{=}0.2), and disable the overlong penalty. Isolates the contribution of DAPO’s full set of drift-enabling modifications.

  • •

    RL-from-base. RL Stage 1 initialised from the un-fine-tuned Qwen3 backbones (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 for the 4B class, Qwen3-1.7B for the 1.7B class), with no SFT at all. Tests whether SFT is necessary before RL.

  • •

    Difficult-only S1. RL Stage 1 trained only on items the size-matched SFT-2 checkpoint fails on every attempt during pass-at-NN annotation (nc=0n_{c}{=}0); 1,2761{,}276 items at 4B and 1,8881{,}888 items at 1.7B. Tests whether training on easy/moderate items is necessary to install short reasoning.

A.17.1  Effectiveness ablations

Mining drives hard-case generalisation.

The clearest effectiveness finding is that the deterministic 1:2 right:wrong mining of Stage 2 (§4.2) accounts for the majority of the Stage-2 lift, and it does so almost entirely through gains on the hardest of our benchmarks (MedXpertQA). Holding the Stage-1 checkpoint and all hyperparameters fixed (Table 36), the mined Stage-2 set lifts MedXpertQA by +6.1+6.1 pp on the 4B model and +4.3+4.3 pp on the 1.7B model, whereas the Random S2 ablation lifts it by only +1.1+1.1 pp and +2.3+2.3 pp respectively. Easy and medium benchmarks (MedQA, PubMedQA) are essentially indistinguishable between mined and random Stage-2 (within the per-benchmark stderr of ∼1.0\sim 1.0 pp). The mined Stage-2 also reaches its peak in fewer steps: for the 4B model the mined run peaks at step 190190, while the random run requires the full 500500 steps to reach a lower plateau.

This pattern matches the design intent: the 1:2 right:wrong subset over-samples failure cases that, by construction, require capabilities beyond surface pattern matching. MedXpertQA requires advanced reasoning patterns to pass; MedQA and PubMedQA are dominated by simpler factual recall and structured-text comprehension, which both Stage-1 RL and even random Stage-2 already saturate.

Reward shape and DAPO group filter are within smoke-eval noise.

The Binary reward ablation, which replaces the four-tier reasoning-aware reward with AlphaMed’s binary {0,1}\{0,1\} correctness reward, leaves average accuracy within ±1.0\pm 1.0 pp of the MedPsy Stage-1 best at both model sizes. The No group filter ablation, which disables DAPO’s dynamic group filtering, is similarly within ±1.0\pm 1.0 pp (Table 38). We do not claim an accuracy contribution from either knob based on these results. The four-tier reward does, however, produce a small but measurable token-efficiency benefit relative to binary, which we attribute to the explicit penalisation of the ‘‘correct without thinking’’ shortcut.55 5 For the 4B model, the average MedQA output tokens at the best checkpoint are 759759 for MedPsy Stage 1 (4-tier reward) vs. 836836 for the Binary reward ablation, about 9%9\% lower for the four-tier reward at matched accuracy. For the 1.7B model the gap is within noise (943943 vs. 944944 tokens).

RL needs SFT.

The RL-from-base ablation initialises RL Stage 1 from the un-fine-tuned Qwen3 backbones (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-1.7B), bypassing both SFT stages. Performance plateaus far below the MedPsy Stage 1 at both model sizes (Table 37): the 4B RL-from-base run reaches a smoke-suite average of 55.89%55.89\% vs. 62.34%62.34\% for the MedPsy Stage 1 (−6.45-6.45 pp), and the 1.7B RL-from-base run reaches 45.07%45.07\% vs. 52.35%52.35\% (−7.28-7.28 pp). Two observations clarify the gap. First, the absolute RL lift over the run’s starting point is comparable to the MedPsy recipe: the 4B RL-from-base run improves from 54.20%54.20\% at step 00 to 55.89%55.89\% at its best step (+1.69+1.69 pp), while MedPsy Stage 1 improves from 60.69%60.69\% to 62.34%62.34\% (+1.65+1.65 pp); both gain ∼1.7\sim 1.7 pp from RL. What differs is the floor, which sits 66–77 pp lower without SFT. Second, the training reward signal in the RL-from-base runs is dominated by missing format compliance: at the 4B size the mean reward converges to ∼0.43\sim 0.43 vs. ∼0.96\sim 0.96 for MedPsy, with the gap explained by the model failing to reliably emit the structured <think>...</think>/<answer>...</answer> format that the SFT pipeline installs (Eq. 1 returns 0.50.5 instead of 1.01.0 even when the answer is correct). We therefore conclude that SFT establishes the operating floor – broad medical coverage and the reasoning-trace format – on top of which RL adds its ∼1.7\sim 1.7 pp of consolidation; RL on the un-fine-tuned backbone is not unable to learn, but cannot recover the SFT-installed capabilities in the same number of optimisation steps. Per-benchmark numbers in Table 37 are consistent with the corresponding backbone numbers reported under LLM-as-Parser in Sec. 5.4 (e.g. MedQA-USMLE on the 4B Qwen3 backbone is 71.56%71.56\% under LLM-as-Parser vs. 72.19%72.19\% for RL-from-base baseline under inspect-ai; MedQA-USMLE on the 1.7B Qwen3 backbone is 47.18%47.18\% under LLM-as-Parser vs. 47.13%47.13\% under inspect-ai).

A.17.2  Token-efficiency ablations: a clean three-way decomposition

The 1.71.7–3.2×3.2\times token-efficiency improvements of the MedPsy models reported in Sec. 5.5 are the most distinctive empirical property of our pipeline. The Vanilla GRPO and No overlong ablations, in combination with the MedPsy runs, decompose this compression into three additive sources, each separately controllable from the others. Table 39 reports per-benchmark average output tokens at the best checkpoint of each variant; Table 40 reports the corresponding training-time response-length trajectory.

Three additive sources.

Reading Table 39 top-to-bottom within each model class:

  • •

    (1) RL with a KL anchor (Vanilla GRPO). Vanilla GRPO compresses MedQA tokens by only 6%6\% on the 4B model and 20%20\% on the 1.7B model relative to the SFT-Stage-2 baseline. The KL anchor pulls the policy back toward the verbose SFT prior, and symmetric clipping limits how far the upper PPO bound can boost short-but-correct trajectories. The accuracy delta of Vanilla GRPO is also small (−0.5-0.5 pp on the 4B model, −0.6-0.6 pp on the 1.7B model vs. the MedPsy Stage 1).

  • •

    (2) DAPO drift modifications (No overlong). Switching to DAPO, removing the KL term and using clip-higher=0.28=0.28, without the overlong penalty pushes compression to 44%44\% (4B) and 45%45\% (1.7B). Allowing the policy to drift further from the SFT prior and biasing the upper PPO bound is responsible for the bulk of the compression, even though neither change references response length explicitly. This ablation also delivers the highest accuracy of any 4B Stage-1 variant (+1.0+1.0 pp vs. MedPsy).

  • •

    (3) The soft overlong-response penalty (MedPsy). Adding the linear penalty over [Lsoft,Lmax][L_{\text{soft}},L_{\text{max}}] on top of DAPO drives compression the rest of the way to 66%66\% (4B) and 65%65\% (1.7B). The overlong penalty contributes its ∼22\sim 22 pp of additional compression with a measured accuracy cost of 1.01.0 pp on the 4B model and 0.80.8 pp on the 1.7B model relative to No overlong; it is also the only component that prevents the right tail of the response-length distribution from re-expanding (Table 40, “Tail (end)” reports the fraction of rollouts at the 4,0964{,}096-token cap). Removing the penalty leaves the mean below LsoftL_{\text{soft}} but allows individual rollouts to grow, increasing average output length at evaluation by approximately 1.6×1.6\times.

The accuracy/efficiency trade-off is modest.

A common concern with length-controlled RL is that compression comes at the cost of accuracy on hard items. In our setting, the measured cost is at most approximately one point on the smoke suite. The No overlong ablation, which keeps DAPO but disables the soft length penalty, scores 63.34%63.34\% avg on the 4B model (vs. 62.34%62.34\% for the MedPsy Stage 1, +1.00+1.00 pp) at the cost of ∼1.6×\sim 1.6\times longer outputs, and 53.15%53.15\% on the 1.7B model (vs. 52.35%52.35\%, +0.80+0.80 pp), again at ∼1.6×\sim 1.6\times length. The overlong penalty therefore buys the headline 1.71.7–3.2×3.2\times token reduction reported in Sec. 5.5 for a worst-case accuracy cost of ∼1\sim 1 pp on the smoke suite. For an on-device deployment this trade-off is decisively in favour of the penalty; for a deployment that prioritises accuracy over latency, dropping the penalty is a defensible alternative.

Why mean tokens shrink even when the penalty is rarely triggered.

A natural objection to the overlong-penalty story is that the policy’s mean response length is well below the Lsoft=2,048L_{\text{soft}}{=}2{,}048-token threshold for almost the entire run, so the penalty should “not matter”. Table 40 resolves this: the penalty does not act on the mean, but on the per-rollout right tail. In the MedPsy runs, the fraction of rollouts that hit the Lmax=4,096L_{\text{max}}{=}4{,}096-token cap drops from 22–3%3\% in the first decile of training to ∼0\sim 0–0.1%0.1\% at the end. Removing the penalty (the No overlong ablation) keeps that tail wide (0.160.16–0.74%0.74\% of rollouts at the cap), and the wider tail in turn pulls the mean upward via DAPO’s drift dynamics. The penalty is best understood as an anchor on the right tail of the response-length distribution, not as a per-step length subtraction.

The full curriculum Pareto-strictly-dominates the single-stage Difficult-only shortcut.

The cleanest counterfactual to the two-stage curriculum is to skip the easy/moderate Stage 1 entirely and run a single RL stage on hard data. The Difficult-only S1 ablation does exactly this: it initializes from the size-matched SFT-2 checkpoint and trains DAPO on only the items the SFT-2 policy fails on every attempt during pass-at-NN annotation (nc=0n_{c}{=}0); the same per-policy mining procedure used to construct the released Stage 2 set. Table 42, Table 41, and Figs. 3–5 compare it to MedPsy S2 (MedPsy = SFT-2 →\to RL Stage 1 on Easy/Moderate →\to RL Stage 2 on mined hard). The result is that every checkpoint along the Difficult-only trajectory is Pareto-dominated by MedPsy S2 on accuracy and training-time response length, simultaneously. At the best-by-accuracy checkpoint MedPsy S2 is better on both axes by a wide margin: +2.69+2.69 pp average accuracy and −1,868-1{,}868 training-time tokens on the 4B model (64.43%64.43\% / 578578 tokens vs. 61.74%61.74\% / 2,4462{,}446 tokens), and +5.90+5.90 pp / −1,515-1{,}515 tokens on the 1.7B model (56.46%56.46\% / 864864 tokens vs. 50.56%50.56\% / 2,3792{,}379 tokens). On the hardest benchmark MedXpertQA the curriculum’s lead widens to +4.33+4.33 pp on the 4B model (31.27%31.27\% vs. 26.94%26.94\%) and +4.82+4.82 pp on the 1.7B model (21.31%21.31\% vs. 16.49%16.49\%).

Why the curriculum wins, and why Difficult-only validates the design.

Fig. 4 traces the training-time mean response length over the full curriculum (the MedPsy trace truncated at the released S2 checkpoint, S2 step 200200 for the 4B model and S2 step 330330 for the 1.7B model). The Easy/Moderate Stage 1 brings the policy from the verbose SFT-2 prior (∼1.8\sim 1.8–2.02.0K tokens) down to ∼620\sim 620–760760 tokens; Stage 2 then trains on hard items starting from that compressed checkpoint and converges to ∼580\sim 580–870870 tokens, gaining accuracy throughout. Difficult-only S1, by contrast, sees no items it can solve at the start of training (every prompt has nc=0n_{c}{=}0 under the SFT-2 policy by construction), so the available reward gradient is dominated by overlong-length and shortcut penalties rather than correctness signal. As a result the policy compresses tokens at essentially the same per-step rate as all DAPO+overlong runs (−65-65% to −77-77% across the run on training-time response length) but loses accuracy as it does so: on the 4B model the run peaks at step 44 (61.74%61.74\%, still close to the SFT-2 starting accuracy of 60.69%60.69\%) and ends at step 100100 at 58.08%58.08\%; on the 1.7B model it peaks at step 44 (50.56%50.56\%) and ends at step 9090 at 47.73%47.73\%. By the end of training, training-time tokens are essentially matched between Difficult-only S1 (∼590\sim 590 on the 4B model, ∼730\sim 730 on the 1.7B model) and MedPsy S2 (578578 / 864864), but accuracy is now 66–99 pp lower. The trajectory therefore validates the design in a stronger form than we initially anticipated: easy/moderate items are necessary not merely to install short reasoning, but to provide a learnable correctness signal at all – a single RL stage on the items the same SFT-2 policy never solves cannot make accuracy progress, and the only thing that does happen with more steps is that the soft-overlong penalty compresses tokens at the cost of accuracy. Easy-first followed by mined hard is what simultaneously installs the short-reasoning habit and gains the hard-item accuracy that defines MedPsy S2.

A note on units.

“Response length” refers to the mean number of tokens the policy emits when it generates a single answer. We report it in two forms that are conceptually the same and differ only in implementation: the training-time value is averaged over the n=16n{=}16 rollouts per training prompt (sampled at temperature 0.70.7 during DAPO group sampling) and is logged every step in W&B; the evaluation value (used in the per-benchmark token tables of Sec. 5.5 and Table 42) is computed over the standard MedQA / MedXpertQA / PubMedQA prompts under deterministic generation. Both views agree on the headline finding (MedPsy S2 Pareto-dominates the Difficult-only trajectory); we use training-time in Figs. 4–3 because it is per-step granular and free of evaluation-prompt confounds.

Would a longer Difficult-only run catch up?

Difficult-only S1 is trained for 5050 epochs (∼100\sim 100 optimisation steps) on the 4B model and 3030 epochs (∼90\sim 90 steps) on the 1.7B model, matched to the MedPsy Stage 1 step count, with each model trained on the items its own size-matched SFT-2 policy fails on every n=5n{=}5 rollout (1,2761{,}276 items at 4B, 1,8881{,}888 at 1.7B). Within the tested budget, two signals argue against near-term catch-up, while the smaller and less diverse training set remains a confound. First, the accuracy trajectory degrades after the first few steps (from 61.74%61.74\% at step 44 down to ∼58\sim 58% on the 4B model; from 50.56%50.56\% at step 44 down to ∼48\sim 48% on the 1.7B model). Second, the training-time response length is approximately saturated by step ∼80\sim 80 at both sizes (∼590\sim 590–650650 tokens on the 4B model, ∼700\sim 700–750750 tokens on the 1.7B model). The observed Difficult-only trajectory is therefore dominated by MedPsy S2 within this training budget; this does not establish a universal result for data-volume-matched or substantially longer runs.

A.17.3  Limitations of these ablations

Three caveats apply. First, all numbers in this appendix are computed on the 3-benchmark smoke-eval suite (MedQA, MedXpertQA, PubMedQA) under the inspect-ai flexible scorer; the per-ablation deltas reproduce under the LLM-as-Parser scorer used for the released checkpoints (Sec. 5.1), but absolute scores differ slightly between the two scorers due to different prompting conventions and post-generation handling. Second, no single ablation in this appendix trains for substantially more compute than the MedPsy component it replaces; we cannot rule out that with 55–10×10\times more steps the gap between mined and random Stage-2, or between MedPsy and No overlong, would close further than reported. Third, the Difficult-only S1 ablation trains on a much smaller and less diverse corpus than MedPsy (1,2761{,}276 items at 4B and 1,8881{,}888 at 1.7B vs. ∼15\sim 15–1616K items in MedPsy Stage 1). We compensate via 5050 vs. 44 epochs (4B) and 3030 vs. 44 epochs (1.7B) to match the MedPsy Stage-1 step count; nevertheless, the diversity of the training distribution remains a confound, and a fully matched-data-volume single-stage comparison is left to future work.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
